Query: What drugs that act on the acetylcholine neurotransmitter system are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease?
Answer: Based on the provided documents, the following drugs that act on the acetylcholine neurotransmitter system are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease: 1. Tacrine: Although it has significant hepatic toxicity, it was the first drug shown to have some benefit in Alzheimer's disease. 2. Donepezil: A newer, more selective acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with less toxicity compared to tacrine. 3. Galantamine: Another newer acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with similar efficacy and lower toxicity compared to tacrine. 4. Rivastigmine: A newer acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with similar efficacy and lower toxicity compared to tacrine. These drugs work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine, thereby increasing the concentration of acetylcholine in the brain. This can help alleviate some symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, such as cognitive dysfunction. However, it's essential to note that the efficacy of these drugs is modest, and they do not prevent the progression of the disease.

Query: Are there any pharmacotherapies targeting the neurotransmitter systems affected in Alzheimer's disease that have shown efficacy in improving cognitive symptoms or slowing disease progression?
Answer: Based on the provided documents, there are several pharmacotherapies that target the neurotransmitter systems affected in Alzheimer's disease, and some have shown efficacy in improving cognitive symptoms or slowing disease progression. Cholinergic precursors and agonists, as well as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil, have been shown to have a modest effect on improving cognitive symptoms and slowing disease progression. According to Document [0], these medications have been demonstrated to prolong the patient's ability to sustain an independent life, with a mean improvement of 2 to 3 points on the Alzheimer Disease Assessment Scale. However, the evidence generally requires that the medications be taken for 6 to 12 months, and the balance of evidence probably favors the use of these medications in practice, but only in mildly or moderately affected patients. N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) glutaminergic antagonists, such as memantine, have also been tried. According to Document [2], memantine has been approved for use in late-stage Alzheimer's disease and in conjunction with cholinergic drugs, and has been shown to have better results on some scales that reflect functional behavior compared to placebo. However, the effects of these drugs in later stages of the disease are minimal. Additionally, Document [3] mentions that recent research has focused on amyloid beta, and several drugs have been developed to target this pathway, including verubecestat, an inhibitor of beta-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme (BACE1). However, it is noted that two anti-amyloid antibodies, solanezumab and bapineuzumab, failed to improve cognition or slow progression in recent clinical trials. It's also worth noting that Document [4] mentions that several trials using small molecule inhibitors of the enzyme γ-secretase, or of an inhibitor of β-site amyloid precursor protein–cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE-1), or of a monoclonal antibody directed at soluble forms of amyloid (solanezumab) have failed to demonstrate clear benefit in even early stages of Alzheimer's disease. In summary, while there are some pharmacotherapies that have shown efficacy in improving cognitive symptoms or slowing disease progression in Alzheimer's disease, the effects are often modest and limited to specific stages of the disease. Further research is needed to develop more effective treatments for this complex and multifactorial disease.

trajectory.question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of increasing forgetfulness over the past 3 years. Initially, he used to forget his children's names or forget to lock the house door. During the past year, he has gotten lost twice while returning from the grocery store and was unable to tell passersby his address. One time, he went to the park with his granddaughter and returned home alone without realizing he had forgotten her. His daughter says that over the past year, he has withdrawn himself from social gatherings and avoids making conversation. He does not sleep well at night. His daughter has hired a helper to cook and clean his home. On mental status examination, he is oriented only to person. He describes his mood as fair. Short- and long-term memory deficits are present. He appears indifferent about his memory lapses and says this is normal for someone his age. The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient is a drug that acts on which of the following neurotransmitters?

Dopaminergic drugs can worsen cognitive function in demented patients and should be stopped or reduced to try and provide a compromise between antiparkinsonian benefit and preserved cognitive function. Drugs are usually discontinued in the following sequence: anticholinergics, amantadine, dopamine agonists, COMT inhibitors, and MAO-B inhibitors. For example, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), which is secreted by the muscle cell into the synaptic cleft, rapidly degrades ACh into acetic acid and choline. Choline is then taken up by the cholinergic presynaptic bouton and reused for ACh synthesis. The AChE action at the neuromuscular junction can be inhibited by various pharmacological compounds, nerve agents, and pesticides resulting in prolonged muscle contraction. Clinically, AChE inhibitors have been used clinically in the treatment of myasthenia gravis (see Folder 11.4 in Chapter 11), a degenerative neuromuscular disorder, glaucoma, and more recently Alzheimer’s disease. These medications have been shown to improve cognitive function in mildly or moderately affected patients, with a mean improvement of 2 to 3 points on the 70-point Alzheimer Disease Assessment Scale. They may also offer a slight prolongation of the patient's ability to sustain an independent life, although this benefit typically requires 6 to 12 months of treatment. However, the limitations of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors include their modest efficacy, potential side effects, and limited benefit in advanced stages of the disease. These medications can cause significant adverse effects, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and other peripheral cholinomimetic effects. Additionally, their benefit is generally limited to mildly or moderately affected patients, and they may not be effective in advanced stages of the disease. Furthermore, the use of these medications requires careful consideration of the potential risks and benefits, as well as regular monitoring for side effects and efficacy. In terms of specific medications, donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine are newer, more selective acetylcholinesterase inhibitors that appear to have the same marginal clinical benefit as tacrine but with less toxicity. Donepezil may be given once daily due to its long half-life and lacks the hepatotoxic effect of tacrine. However, no trials comparing these newer drugs with tacrine have been reported, and their use should be weighed against the need for blood testing and side effects. Overall, the benefits and limitations of using acetylcholinesterase inhibitors as the initial pharmacotherapy for Alzheimer's disease highlight the importance of careful patient selection, regular monitoring, and consideration of alternative treatment options.

iteration_documents.content: Tacrine (tetrahydroaminoacridine, THA), a long-acting cholinesterase inhibitor and muscarinic modulator, was the first drug shown to have any benefit in Alzheimer’s disease. Because of its hepatic toxicity, tacrine has been replaced in clinical use by newer cholinesterase inhibitors: donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine. These agents are orally active, have adequate penetration into the central nervous system, and are much less toxic than tacrine. Although evidence for the benefit of cholinesterase inhibitors (and memantine; see below) is statistically significant, the amount of benefit is modest and does not prevent the progression of the disease. The cholinesterase inhibitors cause significant adverse effects, including nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, and other peripheral cholinomimetic effects. Query: What drugs that act on the acetylcholine neurotransmitter system are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease?

Rivastigmine: A newer acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with similar efficacy and lower toxicity compared to tacrine. These drugs work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine, thereby increasing the concentration of acetylcholine in the brain. This can help alleviate some symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, such as cognitive dysfunction. However, it's essential to note that the efficacy of these drugs is modest, and they do not prevent the progression of the disease.

Inhibitory receptors on NK cells recognize MHC class I molecules on healthy cells, which sends an inhibitory signal that prevents the NK cell from killing the cell. However, when MHC class I expression is downregulated, such as in virus-infected cells or tumor cells, the inhibitory signal is reduced or lost. At the same time, activating receptors on NK cells recognize specific proteins that are increased on the surface of infected cells or tumor cells, which sends an activating signal that stimulates the NK cell to kill the target cell. The balance between these activating and inhibitory signals determines whether the NK cell will kill the target cell. If the activating signals outweigh the inhibitory signals, the NK cell will kill the target cell. This mechanism allows NK cells to selectively target and kill cells that are infected or transformed, while sparing healthy cells. Query: What is the mechanism by which natural killer cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression?
Answer: Natural killer (NK) cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression through a balance of activating and inhibitory signals. Inhibitory receptors on NK cells recognize MHC class I molecules on healthy cells, which sends an inhibitory signal that prevents the NK cell from killing the cell. However, when MHC class I expression is downregulated, such as in virus-infected cells or tumor cells, the inhibitory signal is reduced or lost. At the same time, activating receptors on NK cells recognize specific proteins that are increased on the surface of infected cells or tumor cells, which sends an activating signal that stimulates the NK cell to kill the target cell. The balance between these activating and inhibitory signals determines whether the NK cell will kill the target cell. If the activating signals outweigh the inhibitory signals, the NK cell will kill the target cell. This mechanism allows NK cells to selectively target and kill cells that are infected or transformed, while sparing healthy cells. retrieval_records.query: How do natural killer cells contribute to the prevention of proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: Natural killer (NK) cells play a crucial role in the prevention of proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow through their ability to recognize and eliminate abnormal cells. According to Document [3] (Title: First_Aid_Step1), NK cells are important in innate immunity, especially against intracellular pathogens, and can distinguish between healthy and infected cells by identifying cell surface proteins. In the context of the bone marrow, NK cells can recognize and target monoclonal plasma cells that have undergone malignant transformation, thereby preventing their proliferation. This is supported by Document [4] (Title: InternalMed_Harrison), which mentions that depletion of host NK cells may lower the number of stem cells necessary to reconstitute hematopoiesis, implying that NK cells play a role in regulating the bone marrow environment. Additionally, Document [0] (Title: InternalMed_Harrison) mentions that certain cytokines, such as those that stimulate NK cell proliferation and activation, can also induce apoptosis in target cells, including potentially malignant plasma cells. Overall, the contribution of NK cells to the prevention of proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow is through their ability to recognize and eliminate abnormal cells, thereby maintaining the integrity of the bone marrow environment and preventing the development of malignancies.

Query: What is the mechanism by which natural killer cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression?
Answer: Natural killer (NK) cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression through a balance of activating and inhibitory signals. Inhibitory receptors on NK cells recognize MHC class I molecules on healthy cells, which sends an inhibitory signal that prevents the NK cell from killing the cell. However, when MHC class I expression is downregulated, such as in virus-infected cells or tumor cells, the inhibitory signal is reduced or lost. At the same time, activating receptors on NK cells recognize specific proteins that are increased on the surface of infected cells or tumor cells, which sends an activating signal that stimulates the NK cell to kill the target cell. The balance between these activating and inhibitory signals determines whether the NK cell will kill the target cell. If the activating signals outweigh the inhibitory signals, the NK cell will kill the target cell. This mechanism allows NK cells to selectively target and kill cells that are infected or transformed, while sparing healthy cells. This is described in documents [0], [1], [2], [3], [6], [7], [8], and [9]. Query: What is the role of natural killer cells in recognizing and targeting cells with downregulated MHC class I expression in the context of monoclonal gammopathy?
Answer: Natural killer (NK) cells play a crucial role in recognizing and targeting cells with downregulated MHC class I expression, which is a common strategy used by viruses and some cancer cells to evade the immune system. In the context of monoclonal gammopathy, which is a condition characterized by the proliferation of malignant plasma cells, NK cells can recognize and target these cells for destruction. According to the documents, NK cells have inhibitory receptors that recognize MHC class I molecules on healthy cells, which prevents them from attacking normal cells. However, when MHC class I expression is downregulated on infected or cancerous cells, the inhibitory signals are reduced, allowing the NK cells to recognize and target these cells for destruction (Document 1, Document 4). The documents also mention that NK cells can recognize "missing self" signals, which refer to the reduced expression of MHC class I molecules on the surface of infected or cancerous cells (Document 1, Document 7). This allows NK cells to distinguish between healthy and infected or cancerous cells and target the latter for destruction. In the context of monoclonal gammopathy, NK cells can recognize and target malignant plasma cells that have downregulated MHC class I expression, which is a common feature of many cancer cells (Document 3, Document 5). retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: Natural killer (NK) cells play a crucial role in the elimination of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow through their ability to recognize and kill tumor cells. They achieve this through the release of granular enzymes, such as granzymes and perforins, which create holes in the target cell membrane, leading to cell death. NK cells can also synthesize interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), which inhibits viral infections and stimulates CD4 and CD8 T cell responses. In the context of malignant plasma cells, NK cells can recognize and target these cells for destruction, helping to control tumor growth and progression. However, impaired NK cell function can have significant consequences, including: 1. Reduced tumor cell killing: Impaired NK cell function can lead to a decrease in the ability of NK cells to recognize and kill malignant plasma cells, allowing tumor growth and progression to occur unchecked. 2. Increased risk of disease progression: Impaired NK cell function can increase the risk of disease progression and relapse, as malignant plasma cells are able to evade immune surveillance and continue to proliferate. 3. Decreased response to therapy: Impaired NK cell function can also impact the effectiveness of therapies, such as immunotherapies, that rely on the activation of NK cells to target and kill tumor cells. Overall, the contribution of NK cells to the elimination of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow is critical, and impaired NK cell function can have significant consequences for disease progression and treatment outcomes. Query: What is the mechanism by which natural killer cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression?
Answer: Natural killer (NK) cells recognize and target cells with downregulated MHC class I expression through a balance of activating and inhibitory signals. Inhibitory receptors on NK cells recognize MHC class I molecules on healthy cells, which sends an inhibitory signal that prevents the NK cell from killing the cell. However, when MHC class I expression is downregulated, such as in virus-infected cells or tumor cells, the inhibitory signal is reduced or lost. At the same time, activating receptors on NK cells recognize specific proteins that are increased on the surface of infected cells or tumor cells, which sends an activating signal that stimulates the NK cell to kill the target cell. The balance between these activating and inhibitory signals determines whether the NK cell will kill the target cell. If the activating signals outweigh the inhibitory signals, the NK cell will kill the target cell. This mechanism allows NK cells to selectively target and kill cells that are infected or transformed, while sparing healthy cells. retrieval_records.query: What are the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: Based on the provided documents, the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals can be summarized as follows: 1. **Constitutional delay**: This is a normal variant and the most common cause of delayed puberty. It is often familial and characterized by a delayed bone age and a growth curve that lags behind others of the same age (Document 2, Document 5, Document 8). 2. **Ovarian origin**: Approximately 25-40% of delayed puberty in girls is of ovarian origin, with Turner's syndrome being a common cause (Document 6). 3. **Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This encompasses diverse etiologies such as systemic illnesses (e.g., celiac disease, chronic renal disease), endocrinopathies (e.g., diabetes, hypothyroidism), and decreased energy balance resulting from exercise, dieting, and/or eating disorders (Document 6). 4. **Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes (Document 6, Document 7). 5. **Other causes**: These may include neuroanatomic causes, although they are less common in girls than in boys (Document 7). It's worth noting that a diagnosis of constitutional delay in puberty should only be made after other causes of delayed puberty have been eliminated (Document 5, Document 8).

retrieval_records.query: How does an XY karyotype affect the presentation and development of individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: Individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) have an XY karyotype, which means they have a typical male genetic makeup. However, due to a mutation in the androgen receptor gene, their bodies are unable to respond to androgens (male hormones such as testosterone). As a result, individuals with CAIS develop female external genitalia, despite having testes that produce androgens. The androgens are converted to estrogens, which promote female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development. However, the lack of androgen response also means that these individuals do not develop male secondary sexual characteristics, such as facial hair, pubic hair, or a deep voice. The XY karyotype in individuals with CAIS also means that they do not have a uterus or other female internal reproductive organs, as these are typically developed in response to the presence of two X chromosomes. Instead, they may have a short, blind-ending vagina and no internal müllerian structures. At puberty, individuals with CAIS typically develop breasts and may appear to be phenotypically female. However, they do not experience menstruation and may not develop pubic or axillary hair. The testes, which are usually located in the inguinal canal or labia majora, produce androgens, but these have no effect on the individual's development due to the androgen insensitivity. Overall, the XY karyotype in individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to a unique presentation and development, with a mix of female and male characteristics, but ultimately resulting in a female phenotype due to the lack of androgen response.

Pathological puberty delay: Rarely, due to systemic disease (e.g., IBD), malnutrition (e.g., anorexia nervosa), gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Klinefelter’s syndrome, Turner’s syndrome), or endocrine abnormalities (e.g., hypopituitarism, hypothyroidism, Kallmann’s syndrome, androgen insensitivity syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome) Precocious puberty: Any sign of 2° sexual maturation in girls < 8 years or boys < 9 years of age. Often idiopathic; may be central or peripheral (see the Gynecology chapter).

iteration_documents.content: The complete form of androgen resistance or androgen insensitivity syndrome is the most dramatic example of resistance to hormone action by defects in the androgen receptor. Affected patients have a 46,XY karyotype, normally formed testes (usually located in the inguinal canal or labia majora), and female external genitalia with a short vagina and no internal müllerian structures. At the time of puberty, testosterone concentrations increase to normal or above normal male range. Because a portion of the testosterone is normally converted to estradiol in peripheral tissues and the estrogen cannot be opposed by the androgen, breast development ensues at the normal age of puberty without growth of pubic, facial, or axillary hair or the occurrence of menstruation.

Query: What are the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals?
Answer: Based on the provided documents, the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals can be summarized as follows: 1. **Constitutional delay**: This is a normal variant and the most common cause of delayed puberty. It is often familial and characterized by a delayed bone age and a growth curve that lags behind others of the same age (Document 2, Document 5, Document 8). 2. **Ovarian origin**: Approximately 25-40% of delayed puberty in girls is of ovarian origin, with Turner's syndrome being a common cause (Document 6). 3. **Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This encompasses diverse etiologies such as systemic illnesses (e.g., celiac disease, chronic renal disease), endocrinopathies (e.g., diabetes, hypothyroidism), and decreased energy balance resulting from exercise, dieting, and/or eating disorders (Document 6). 4. **Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes (Document 6, Document 7). 5. **Other causes**: These may include neuroanatomic causes, although they are less common in girls than in boys (Document 7). It's worth noting that a diagnosis of constitutional delay in puberty should only be made after other causes of delayed puberty have been eliminated (Document 5, Document 8).

Query: How does an XY karyotype affect the presentation and development of individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome?
Answer: Individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) have an XY karyotype, which means they have a typical male genetic makeup. However, due to a mutation in the androgen receptor gene, their bodies are unable to respond to androgens (male hormones such as testosterone). As a result, individuals with CAIS develop female external genitalia, despite having testes that produce androgens. The androgens are converted to estrogens, which promote female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development. However, the lack of androgen response also means that these individuals do not develop male secondary sexual characteristics, such as facial hair, pubic hair, or a deep voice. The XY karyotype in individuals with CAIS also means that they do not have a uterus or other female internal reproductive organs, as these are typically developed in response to the presence of two X chromosomes. Instead, they may have a short, blind-ending vagina and no internal müllerian structures. At puberty, individuals with CAIS typically develop breasts and may appear to be phenotypically female. However, they do not experience menstruation and may not develop pubic or axillary hair. The testes, which are usually located in the inguinal canal or labia majora, produce androgens, but these have no effect on the individual's development due to the androgen insensitivity. Overall, the XY karyotype in individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to a unique presentation and development, with a mix of female and male characteristics, but ultimately resulting in a female phenotype due to the lack of androgen response.

retrieval_records.query: How does constitutional delay affect the presentation and development of puberty in genetically female individuals?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: According to the provided documents, constitutional delay in genetically female individuals (girls) affects the presentation and development of puberty in the following ways: 1. **Delayed onset of pubertal development**: Girls with constitutional delay will experience a delayed onset of pubertal development, which means they will start developing secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development and pubic hair, later than their peers (Document [0], Document [1], and Document [5]). 2. **Delayed bone age**: The bone age of girls with constitutional delay is typically delayed, meaning their skeletal maturity is behind that of their chronological age (Document [1] and Document [4]). 3. **Normal growth velocity**: Despite the delayed onset of puberty, girls with constitutional delay usually have a normal growth velocity, although it may be below the normal percentiles on the growth curve (Document [1] and Document [5]). 4. **Family history**: A family history of delayed puberty is common in girls with constitutional delay, and their parents may have also experienced delayed growth or puberty (Document [1] and Document [5]). 5. **Normal adult height**: Girls with constitutional delay typically achieve a normal adult height, consistent with their genetic potential, although it may be lower than average (Document [1] and Document [5]). 6. **Delayed menarche**: Girls with constitutional delay may experience delayed menarche (first menstrual period), which can occur later than in their peers (Document [7]). It's essential to note that constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other underlying pathologic processes must be ruled out before making this diagnosis (Document [3] and Document [9]).

iteration_documents.content: The complete form of androgen resistance or androgen insensitivity syndrome is the most dramatic example of resistance to hormone action by defects in the androgen receptor. trajectory.context:
Query: What are the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals?
Answer: Based on the provided documents, the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals can be summarized as follows: 1. **Constitutional delay**: This is a normal variant and the most common cause of delayed puberty. It is often familial and characterized by a delayed bone age and a growth curve that lags behind others of the same age (Document 2, Document 5, Document 8). 2. **Ovarian origin**: Approximately 25-40% of delayed puberty in girls is of ovarian origin, with Turner's syndrome being a common cause (Document 6). 3. **Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This encompasses diverse etiologies such as systemic illnesses (e.g., celiac disease, chronic renal disease), endocrinopathies (e.g., diabetes, hypothyroidism), and decreased energy balance resulting from exercise, dieting, and/or eating disorders (Document 6). 4. **Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes (Document 6, Document 7). 5. **Other causes**: These may include neuroanatomic causes, although they are less common in girls than in boys (Document 7). It's worth noting that a diagnosis of constitutional delay in puberty should only be made after other causes of delayed puberty have been eliminated (Document 5, Document 8).

Query: How does an XY karyotype affect the presentation and development of individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome?
Answer: Individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) have an XY karyotype, which means they have a typical male genetic makeup. However, due to a mutation in the androgen receptor gene, their bodies are unable to respond to androgens (male hormones such as testosterone). As a result, individuals with CAIS develop female external genitalia, despite having testes that produce androgens. The androgens are converted to estrogens, which promote female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development. However, the lack of androgen response also means that these individuals do not develop male secondary sexual characteristics, such as facial hair, pubic hair, or a deep voice. The XY karyotype in individuals with CAIS also means that they do not have a uterus or other female internal reproductive organs, as these are typically developed in response to the presence of two X chromosomes. Instead, they may have a short, blind-ending vagina and no internal müllerian structures. At puberty, individuals with CAIS typically develop breasts and may appear to be phenotypically female. However, they do not experience menstruation and may not develop pubic or axillary hair. The testes, which are usually located in the inguinal canal or labia majora, produce androgens, but these have no effect on the individual's development due to the androgen insensitivity. Overall, the XY karyotype in individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to a unique presentation and development, with a mix of female and male characteristics, but ultimately resulting in a female phenotype due to the lack of androgen response.

Query: What are the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals with normal external and internal genitalia?
Answer: Based on the provided documents, the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals with normal external and internal genitalia can be attributed to various factors. Document [2] (Title: Gynecology_Novak) mentions that at least 17 different single-gene mutations are identified as being associated with delayed or absent puberty in humans. These genes include KAL1 (X-linked Kallmann syndrome), FGFR1 (autosomal Kallmann syndrome), DAX1 (the gene for X-linked congenital adrenal hypoplasia), GNRHR (the gene for the GnRH receptor), PC1 (the gene for prohormone convertase 1), and GPR54 (encoding a G-protein coupled receptor). Document [5] (Title: InternalMed_Harrison) states that congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in girls or boys can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes. Approximately 50% of girls with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, with or without anosmia, have a history of some degree of breast development, and 10% report one to two episodes of vaginal bleeding. Document [7] (Title: Gynecology_Novak) classifies aberrations of pubertal development in girls into four broad categories, including delayed or interrupted puberty, which can be caused by anatomic abnormalities of the genital outflow tract, gonadal dysgenesis, early gonadal "failure" with apparent normal ovarian development, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. In summary, the common causes of delayed puberty in genetically female individuals with normal external and internal genitalia include: 1. Single-gene mutations (e.g., KAL1, FGFR1, DAX1, GNRHR, PC1, and GPR54) 2. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 3. Anatomic abnormalities of the genital outflow tract 4. Gonadal dysgenesis 5. Early gonadal "failure" with apparent normal ovarian development 6. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism These causes can lead to delayed or absent puberty in genetically female individuals with normal external and internal genitalia.

Query: How does constitutional delay affect the presentation and development of puberty in genetically female individuals?
Answer: According to the provided documents, constitutional delay in genetically female individuals (girls) affects the presentation and development of puberty in the following ways: 1. **Delayed onset of pubertal development**: Girls with constitutional delay will experience a delayed onset of pubertal development, which means they will start developing secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development and pubic hair, later than their peers (Document [0], Document [1], and Document [5]). 2. **Delayed bone age**: The bone age of girls with constitutional delay is typically delayed, meaning their skeletal maturity is behind that of their chronological age (Document [1] and Document [4]). 3. **Normal growth velocity**: Despite the delayed onset of puberty, girls with constitutional delay usually have a normal growth velocity, although it may be below the normal percentiles on the growth curve (Document [1] and Document [5]). 4. **Family history**: A family history of delayed puberty is common in girls with constitutional delay, and their parents may have also experienced delayed growth or puberty (Document [1] and Document [5]). 5. **Normal adult height**: Girls with constitutional delay typically achieve a normal adult height, consistent with their genetic potential, although it may be lower than average (Document [1] and Document [5]). 6. **Delayed menarche**: Girls with constitutional delay may experience delayed menarche (first menstrual period), which can occur later than in their peers (Document [7]). It's essential to note that constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other underlying pathologic processes must be ruled out before making this diagnosis (Document [3] and Document [9]).

trajectory.question: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her father for evaluation. retrieval_records.query: How does constitutional delay affect the presentation and development of puberty in genetically female individuals?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: According to the provided documents, constitutional delay in genetically female individuals (girls) affects the presentation and development of puberty in the following ways: 1. **Delayed onset of pubertal development**: Girls with constitutional delay will experience a delayed onset of pubertal development, which may not start until a later age (Document [1]: "Spontaneous puberty usually begins in these patients by the time the bone age reaches 12 years in boys and 11 years in girls"). 2. **Delayed bone age**: The bone age of girls with constitutional delay is typically delayed, which means that their skeletal maturity is not consistent with their chronological age (Document [1]: "significant bone age delay (2 standard deviations below the mean, which is equal to a 1.5to 2-year delay as a teenager)"). 3. **Normal growth velocity**: Despite the delayed onset of puberty, girls with constitutional delay usually have a normal growth velocity, although it may be below the normal percentiles on the growth curve (Document [1]: "Usually height gain is below, although fairly parallel to, the normal percentiles on the growth curve"). 4. **Family history**: A family history of delayed puberty is common in girls with constitutional delay, and their parents may have also experienced delayed growth or puberty (Document [5]: "Usually a family member had delayed growth or puberty but achieved a normal final height"). 5. **Normal adult height**: Girls with constitutional delay typically achieve a normal adult height, consistent with their genetic potential, although it may be reached at a later age (Document [1]: "Adult height normal for the genetic potential is generally attained"). 6. **Delayed secondary sexual development**: Constitutional delay can lead to a delay in secondary sexual development, such as breast development and pubic hair growth (Document [5]: "Constitutional delay usually leads to a delay in secondary sexual development"). It's essential to note that constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other underlying pathologic processes must be ruled out before making this diagnosis (Document [3]: "Constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires ongoing evaluation until the onset of puberty and the growth spurt").

iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: Reassurance without hormonal treatment is appropriate for many individuals with presumed constitutional delay of puberty. However, the impact of delayed growth and pubertal progression on a child’s social relationships and school performance should be weighed. Also, boys with constitutional delay of puberty are less likely to achieve their full genetic height potential and have reduced total-body bone mass as adults, mainly due to narrow limb bones and vertebrae as a result of impaired periosteal expansion during puberty. Administration of androgen therapy to boys with constitutional delay does not affect final height, and when administered with an aromatase inhibitor, it may improve final height.

iteration_documents.title: Gynecology_Novak
iteration_documents.content: At least 17 different single-gene mutations are identified as being associated with delayed or absent puberty in humans (51). They are estimated to account for about 30% of individuals with disorders of puberty. These genes include KAL1 (X-linked Kallmann syndrome), FGFR1 (autosomal Kallmann syndrome), DAX1 (the gene for X-linked congenital adrenal hypoplasia), GNRHR (the gene for the GnRH receptor), PC1 (the gene for prohormone convertase 1), and GPR54 (encoding a G-protein coupled receptor). Delayed puberty may result from mutations in genes affecting gonadotrophs specifically (GnRHR, LHβ, FSHβ) or in genes involved more generally in the development and functioning of the pituitary gland (LHX3, PROP1, HESX1).

iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: Delayed Puberty Delayed puberty (Table 412-4) is defined as the absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age 13 in girls. The diagnostic considerations are very similar to those for primary amenorrhea (Chap. 69). Between 25 and 40% of delayed puberty in girls is of ovarian origin, with Turner’s syndrome accounting for the majority of such patients. Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism encompasses diverse etiologies such as systemic illnesses, including celiac disease and chronic renal disease, and endocrinopathies such as diabetes and hypothyroidism. In addition, girls appear to be particularly susceptible to the adverse effects of decreased energy balance resulting from exercise, dieting, and/or eating disorders. Together these reversible conditions account for ~25% of delayed puberty in girls. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in girls or boys can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes (Fig. 412-4, Chap. 411, Table 411-2).

It is often familial and characterized by a delayed bone age and a growth curve that lags behind others of the same age (Document 2, Document 5, Document 8). 2. **Ovarian origin**: Approximately 25-40% of delayed puberty in girls is of ovarian origin, with Turner's syndrome being a common cause (Document 6). 3. **Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This encompasses diverse etiologies such as systemic illnesses (e.g., celiac disease, chronic renal disease), endocrinopathies (e.g., diabetes, hypothyroidism), and decreased energy balance resulting from exercise, dieting, and/or eating disorders (Document 6). 4. **Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism**: This can be caused by mutations in several different genes or combinations of genes (Document 6, Document 7). 5. **Other causes**: These may include neuroanatomic causes, although they are less common in girls than in boys (Document 7). It's worth noting that a diagnosis of constitutional delay in puberty should only be made after other causes of delayed puberty have been eliminated (Document 5, Document 8).

Query: How does an XY karyotype affect the presentation and development of individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome?
Answer: Individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) have an XY karyotype, which means they have a typical male genetic makeup. However, due to a mutation in the androgen receptor gene, their bodies are unable to respond to androgens (male hormones such as testosterone). As a result, individuals with CAIS develop female external genitalia, despite having testes that produce androgens. The androgens are converted to estrogens, which promote female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development. However, the lack of androgen response also means that these individuals do not develop male secondary sexual characteristics, such as facial hair, pubic hair, or a deep voice. The XY karyotype in individuals with CAIS also means that they do not have a uterus or other female internal reproductive organs, as these are typically developed in response to the presence of two X chromosomes. Instead, they may have a short, blind-ending vagina and no internal müllerian structures. At puberty, individuals with CAIS typically develop breasts and may appear to be phenotypically female. However, they do not experience menstruation and may not develop pubic or axillary hair. The testes, which are usually located in the inguinal canal or labia majora, produce androgens, but these have no effect on the individual's development due to the androgen insensitivity. Overall, the XY karyotype in individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to a unique presentation and development, with a mix of female and male characteristics, but ultimately resulting in a female phenotype due to the lack of androgen response.

retrieved_documents.content: The structural abnormalities known as the congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUTs) are a group of etiologically and phenotypically heterogeneous disorders. Some form of CAKUT is estimated to occur in up to 1 in 500 live births. Specific abnormalities classified as part of the CAKUT spectrum include kidney hypoplasia, kidney agenesis, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and vesicoureteral reflux. CAKUT can be the cause of clinically significant problems in both adults and children. However, it is a major contributor to kidney failure in children, accounting for more than one-third of end-stage kidney disease in this group.

retrieved_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
retrieved_documents.content: CAKUT is typically a sporadic finding but can also cluster in families. Familial forms can be observed as parts of multisystem developmental syndromes. A growing list of specific genes have been identified, which when mutated lead to syndromic forms of CAKUT. For example, the branchio-oto-renal syndrome, characterized by developmental abnormalities in the neck, ears, and kidney, can be caused by mutations in the EYA1 and SIX1 genes. Mutations in the PAX2 transcription factor gene can cause the autosomal dominant renal coloboma syndrome, characterized by optic nerve malformations and hypoplastic kidneys. In many instances, CAKUT is caused by environmental influences rather than genetic alterations. For example, renal tubular dysgenesis, defined by altered tubule development, can be caused by prenatal exposure to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers.

iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: The structural abnormalities known as the congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUTs) are a group of etiologically and phenotypically heterogeneous disorders. Some form of CAKUT is estimated to occur in up to 1 in 500 live births. Specific abnormalities classified as part of the CAKUT spectrum include kidney hypoplasia, kidney agenesis, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and vesicoureteral reflux. CAKUT can be the cause of clinically significant problems in both adults and children. However, it is a major contributor to kidney failure in children, accounting for more than one-third of end-stage kidney disease in this group.

iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: CAKUT is typically a sporadic finding but can also cluster in families. Familial forms can be observed as parts of multisystem developmental syndromes. A growing list of specific genes have been identified, which when mutated lead to syndromic forms of CAKUT. For example, the branchio-oto-renal syndrome, characterized by developmental abnormalities in the neck, ears, and kidney, can be caused by mutations in the EYA1 and SIX1 genes. Mutations in the PAX2 transcription factor gene can cause the autosomal dominant renal coloboma syndrome, characterized by optic nerve malformations and hypoplastic kidneys. In many instances, CAKUT is caused by environmental influences rather than genetic alterations. For example, renal tubular dysgenesis, defined by altered tubule development, can be caused by prenatal exposure to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers.

Decreased sodium excretion causes an obligatory increase in fluid volume and increased cardiac output, thereby elevating blood pressure (see Fig. 10.3 ). At the new higher blood pressure, the kidneys excrete additional sodium. Thus, a new steady state of sodium excretion is achieved, but at the expense of an elevated blood pressure. retrieval_records.query: How does horseshoe kidney, a common renal abnormality in Turner syndrome, affect blood pressure regulation and contribute to the development of hypertension?
retrieval_records.intermediate_answer: Based on the provided documents, there is no direct information about the specific effect of horseshoe kidney on blood pressure regulation and the development of hypertension. However, we can make some inferences based on the general information about kidney function and hypertension. Document [3] (Title: InternalMed_Harrison) mentions that primary renal disease is the most common etiology of secondary hypertension, and mechanisms of kidney-related hypertension include a diminished capacity to excrete sodium, excessive renin secretion in relation to volume status, and sympathetic nervous system overactivity. Document [6] (Title: Pathology_Robbins) explains that the kidneys influence peripheral resistance and sodium excretion/retention primarily through the renin-angiotensin system. The kidneys and heart contain cells that sense changes in blood pressure and/or blood volume, and in response, these cells release several important regulators that act in concert to maintain normal blood pressure. Horseshoe kidney, a common renal abnormality in Turner syndrome, may affect blood pressure regulation by altering the normal functioning of the kidneys. The abnormal kidney structure and function may lead to a diminished capacity to excrete sodium, excessive renin secretion, or altered sympathetic nervous system activity, which can contribute to the development of hypertension. However, without specific information about the effects of horseshoe kidney on blood pressure regulation, it is difficult to provide a more detailed explanation. Further research and studies would be necessary to fully understand the relationship between horseshoe kidney and hypertension.

retrieved_documents.title: Pathology_Robbins
retrieved_documents.content: Although the specific triggers are unknown, it appears that both altered renal sodium handling and increased vascular resistance contribute to essential hypertension. Reduced renal sodium excretion in the presence of normal arterial pressure probably is a key pathogenic feature; indeed, this is a common etiologic factor in most forms of hypertension. Decreased sodium excretion causes an obligatory increase in fluid volume and increased cardiac output, thereby elevating blood pressure (see Fig. 10.3 ). At the new higher blood pressure, the kidneys excrete additional sodium. Thus, a new steady state of sodium excretion is achieved, but at the expense of an elevated blood pressure. Increased vascular resistance may stem from vasoconstriction or structural changes in vessel walls. These are not necessarily independent factors, as chronic vasoconstriction may result in permanent thickening of the walls of affected vessels.

retrieved_documents.content: NaCl-dependent hypertension may be a consequence of a decreased capacity of the kidney to excrete sodium, due either to intrinsic renal disease or to increased production of a salt-retaining hormone (mineralocorticoid) resulting in increased renal tubular reabsorption of sodium. Renal tubular sodium reabsorption also may be augmented by increased neural activity to the kidney. In each of these situations, a higher arterial pressure may be required to achieve sodium balance. Conversely, salt-wasting disorders are associated with low blood pressure levels. ESRD is an extreme example of volume-dependent hypertension. In ~80% of these patients, vascular volume and hypertension can be controlled with adequate dialysis; in the other 20%, the mechanism of hypertension is related to increased activity of the reninangiotensin system and is likely to be responsive to pharmacologic blockade of renin-angiotensin.

retrieved_documents.content: With increased blood flow to the kidney, there is glomerular hypertension (i.e., an increase in glomerular capillary pressure). There is increased wall tension and force on the capillary wall that is counteracted by contractile properties of the endothelium and elastic properties of the glomerular basement membrane. The force is conveyed to podocytes, which adapt by reinforcing cell cycle arrest and increasing cell adhesion in an adaptive attempt to maintain the delicate architecture of the interdigitating foot processes. Over time, however, these increased forces due to glomerular hypertension lead to podocyte damage and glomerulosclerosis. retrieved_documents.content: Preliminary evidence suggests that there may also be genetic determinants of target organ damage attributed to hypertension. Family studies indicate significant heritability of left ventricular mass, and there is considerable individual variation in the responses of the heart to hypertension. Family studies and variations in candidate genes associated with renal damage suggest that genetic factors also may contribute to hypertensive nephropathy. Specific genetic variants have been linked to CHD and stroke. In the future, it is possible that DNA analysis will predict individual risk for hypertension and target organ damage and will identify responders to specific classes of antihypertensive agents. However, with the exception of the rare, monogenic hypertensive diseases, the genetic variants associated with hypertension remain to be confirmed, and the intermediate steps by which these variants affect blood pressure remain to be determined.

iteration_documents.content: With increased blood flow to the kidney, there is glomerular hypertension (i.e., an increase in glomerular capillary pressure). There is increased wall tension and force on the capillary wall that is counteracted by contractile properties of the endothelium and elastic properties of the glomerular basement membrane. The force is conveyed to podocytes, which adapt by reinforcing cell cycle arrest and increasing cell adhesion in an adaptive attempt to maintain the delicate architecture of the interdigitating foot processes. Over time, however, these increased forces due to glomerular hypertension lead to podocyte damage and glomerulosclerosis. iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: Preliminary evidence suggests that there may also be genetic determinants of target organ damage attributed to hypertension. Family studies indicate significant heritability of left ventricular mass, and there is considerable individual variation in the responses of the heart to hypertension. Family studies and variations in candidate genes associated with renal damage suggest that genetic factors also may contribute to hypertensive nephropathy. Specific genetic variants have been linked to CHD and stroke. In the future, it is possible that DNA analysis will predict individual risk for hypertension and target organ damage and will identify responders to specific classes of antihypertensive agents. However, with the exception of the rare, monogenic hypertensive diseases, the genetic variants associated with hypertension remain to be confirmed, and the intermediate steps by which these variants affect blood pressure remain to be determined.

iteration_documents.title: InternalMed_Harrison
iteration_documents.content: Although cigarette smoking is the cause of the majority of lung cancers, several other risk factors have been identified, including occupational exposures to asbestos, arsenic, bischloromethyl ether, hexavalent chromium, mustard gas, nickel (as in certain nickel-refining processes), and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Occupational observations also have provided insight into possible mechanisms of lung cancer induction. For example, the risk of lung cancer among asbestos-exposed workers is increased primarily among those with underlying asbestosis, raising the possibility that the scarring and inflammation produced by this fibrotic nonmalignant lung disease may in many cases (although likely not in all) be the trigger for asbestos-induced lung cancer. Several other occupational exposures have been associated with increased rates of lung cancer, but the causal nature of the association is not as clear.
